items.title: Australian coral reefs face risk of collapse within 50 years without drastic action, global assessment finds
items.summary: Every shallow-water coral reef ecosystem in Australia faces an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075, driven largely by projected ocean warming, according to a global assessment.

items.title: Crows make decisions twice as fast as humans and monkeys
items.summary: University of Tübingen researchers have shown that crows, when confronted with a visual choice, make a decision twice as fast as humans and monkeys. items.title: Storms batter Europe, hitting power supplies, flights and phones
items.summary: Storms battered northern Europe on Sunday, cutting power to more than 150,000 homes, forcing the cancellation of hundreds of flights and silencing phone networks.

items.title: Monarchs report their locations via… cellphone?
items.summary: Who knew a monarch butterfly could borrow a cellphone to check in with friendly people he met on his journey? That is essentially what happens now that new technology has reduced the weight of a radio-pulse tag to less than half a gram (0.02 ounces).

items.title: Milky Way's disk grew 'upside down,' with younger stars forming in ever-thinner layers
items.summary: The Milky Way is home to hundreds of billions of stars arranged in a glorious spiral pattern. But beyond the obvious spiral, our galaxy has other physical characteristics. It's divided into a galactic bulge, a galactic disk and a galactic halo.

items.title: How screening tools measure disadvantage may leave rural communities overlooked for public support
items.summary: Whether a community is prioritized for public support can depend on how its needs are measured, according to new research from the University of New Hampshire. items.summary: A team at HZB has, for the first time, reported polar vortices in (BaTiO₃/SrTiO₃)₁₀ superlattices on silicon. items.title: Protecting children from harm isn't enough—welfare systems must support healing through quality mental health care
items.summary: In Quebec and across Canada, people working in child welfare do remarkable work to protect children and youth from maltreatment and to support families facing complex challenges.

items.title: A few seconds of loading time can push online learners off track
items.summary: An online lesson takes an extra second to load. The wait may seem trivial, but in a study examining large learning platforms, these brief pauses were linked to unfinished assignments, lower scores and less time spent on the site.

items.title: Microorganisms show promise for reducing emissions from manure
items.summary: Dairy farmers sometimes use additives in their cattle housing to reduce emissions from slurry. Emissions of substances such as ammonia occur when urine and feces mix on the floor of the housing. items.title: Southern Africa's first known stenciled rock art found hiding in plain sight
items.summary: Southern Africa has one of the most detailed and elaborate bodies of rock art anywhere in the world, from herds of running antelope to dancing men and humanoid beings with wings, hooves and horns. All are painted with fine brushstrokes or fingers. One thing this art lacks is stencils.

items.summary: Missing blood pressure medication could mean losing much of its protection against heart attacks and strokes, according to an analysis of more than 91,000 people. items.title: Just two drinks a day may be far riskier than you think
items.summary: A major new study reveals that drinking just two alcoholic beverages a day is associated with a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of death from alcohol-related causes, challenging the idea that moderate drinking is harmless. items.title: New evidence suggests spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater
items.summary: Millions of years after animals first conquered land, some took an extraordinary evolutionary U-turn and returned to the water. items.title: Scientists discover how pancreatic cancer rewrites its DNA to escape treatment
items.summary: Scientists have discovered how pancreatic cancer cells continually reshape their genetic makeup to become more aggressive, spread, and evade treatment. In laboratory experiments, blocking a key gene reversed some of these dangerous changes, revealing a potential new way to fight the deadly disease.

items.title: Sea cucumber–inspired gel could help heal damaged tissue in humans
items.summary: Inspired by the ability of sea cucumbers to change the stiffness of their bodies, University of Waterloo researchers have developed a gel that could one day help repair damaged tendons and other soft tissues without leaving permanent material behind.

items.summary: A common, inexpensive medication could hold an unexpected clue to preventing dementia. items.summary: In 1987, biologists captured the last free-flying condor to transfer it to captivity, and the largest flying North American bird species was officially declared extinct in the wild. items.title: Bell pepper colors reveal differences in sweetness, nutrients and ripeness
items.summary: Raw, grilled, roasted, stuffed—there are many ways to enjoy bell peppers, also called capsicums, sweet peppers or paprika. Bell peppers originated in Central and South America and belong to the nightshade family along with tomatoes and eggplants.

items.title: Tests reveal why titanium additions do not fully prevent pitting corrosion in stainless steel
items.summary: Stainless steel is widely used for its corrosion resistance, but it is not invincible. In environments containing chloride ions, such as seawater, pitting corrosion can occur. These pits often start at tiny particles called inclusions embedded in the steel.
